statement: In drivers, a positive test for recent cannabis, compared with a negative test, is associated with higher odds of being in a crash or of being judged responsible for one. Across 28 estimates from 21 case-control and culpability studies in 13 countries (1982–2015), the pooled odds ratio was 1.36 (95% CI 1.15–1.61) by random effects and 1.22 (1.10–1.36) by a regression that corrects for small-study effects (PEESE). A 2012 meta-analysis of nine studies reported 1.92 (1.35–2.73) from crude counts; for those nine studies the re-analysis found a lower value, which its authors say lies between the two pooled figures, after re-extracting counts, using adjusted estimates and correcting for the culpability design. The size depends on how alcohol was handled: 1.11 (1.04–1.18) and 1.18 (1.07–1.30) in the 14 estimates that controlled for alcohol, against 1.79 (1.28–2.51) and 1.69 (1.25–2.28) in the 14 that did not. Individual estimates range from 0.22 to 13.40, with 17 above 1 and 9 below (editors' count), and no heterogeneity statistic is printed. The heaviest single weight (10.68%) is a US analysis of 150,010 drivers tested after fatal crashes, listed at 1.10 (1.02–1.18) as a culpability study; its own adjusted odds ratio for a recorded unsafe driver action with THC alone was 1.165 (1.082–1.255), and for the driver it modelled (a 45-year-old man with no other drugs or driving record) the share with a recorded unsafe action rose from about 52 to 56 in 100 with THC (editors' calculation). These sources are not independent: the 2016 analysis re-analyses the nine studies of the 2012 review and includes the 2015 US study, so they count once. The odds ratios compare crashed with non-crashed drivers, or at-fault with not-at-fault crashed drivers, so they give no chance of a crash for any one driver; a positive test shows cannabis in the body (in blood, saliva or urine, depending on the study), not impairment; most estimates come from studies with limited adjustment; the re-analysis authors say remaining selection effects may bias the figures in either direction; and cause is not shown.
plain: Are drivers with cannabis in their body more often in crashes? Across 28 results from 21 studies, drivers with recent cannabis found in a blood, saliva or urine test had about 1.2 to 1.4 times the odds of being in a crash, or of being at fault in one, compared with drivers without it. An older review found about 1.9 times; re-checking its counts and allowing for other things brought the same studies to between 1.2 and 1.4. When the studies allowed for alcohol, the figure was about 1.1 to 1.2. These studies compare crashed drivers with other drivers, so they cannot give the chance that any one driver crashes, and a positive test shows cannabis was in the body, not that a driver was impaired.
population: Drivers in motor vehicle crashes and comparison drivers in 13 countries (United States, Australia, France, Canada, Norway, New Zealand, Netherlands, Thailand, Belgium, Denmark, Italy, Lithuania, Portugal), 1982–2015: 28 estimates from 21 case-control or culpability studies (239,739 drivers in the pooled studies), including a US analysis of 150,010 tested drivers in fatal crashes
exposure: A positive laboratory test for recent cannabis (blood, saliva or urine, or a mix, depending on the study; self-report in one)
comparator: A negative test (drivers without cannabis detected)
outcome: Being in a crash (case-control studies) or being judged responsible for a crash (culpability studies); in the US analysis, a recorded unsafe driver action
magnitude: Pooled odds ratios, 28 estimates from 21 studies (Rogeberg and Elvik, 2016; random effects; PEESE small-study regression; PEESE bias test P = 0.52; trimmed mean 1.23): 1.36 (1.15–1.61); 1.22 (1.10–1.36). Alcohol controlled (14 estimates) 1.11 (1.04–1.18) and 1.18 (1.07–1.30); not controlled (14) 1.79 (1.28–2.51) and 1.69 (1.25–2.28). High confounder adjustment (11) 1.17 (1.04–1.33) and 1.18 (1.06–1.31); limited or no adjustment (17) 1.52 (1.07–2.15) and 1.70 (1.19–2.41). Case-control (17) 1.60 and 1.32; culpability (11) 1.12 and 1.20. By quality of the measure of use: low (7) 1.07 and 1.08, medium (9) 1.81 and 1.90, high (12) 1.37 and 1.20. Study estimates 0.22 to 13.40; 17 above 1 (7 with intervals excluding 1, among them Laumon 1.43, Li 1.84, Brault 1.60 and Dubois 1.10), 9 below 1 (none excluding 1) and 2 at 1.00, editors' count from the forest plot. Earlier estimate (Asbridge et al., 2012; nine studies, crude counts, drivers with THC and no alcohol or other drug): 1.92 (1.35–2.73), I-squared 81%. Re-extraction changed four of the nine odds ratios by more than 10%, all downwards (for example 7.2 to 2.6 and 4.4 to 1.7); the revised pooled value for the same nine studies was about 1.6 with corrected counts and about 1.25–1.3 with adjusted estimates and the culpability correction (read by eye from a figure; approximate), and the authors say it lies between 1.22 and 1.36. No absolute risk is available: the studies compare crashed with non-crashed drivers or at-fault with not-at-fault drivers. If the odds ratios stood for a causal effect, (odds ratio − 1) divided by the odds ratio would give about 18 and 26 in 100 crashes involving a positive test (editors' calculation for 1.22 and 1.36; the authors say roughly 20 to 30 in 100). In the US analysis of drivers in fatal crashes (Dubois et al., 2015), THC alone at blood alcohol 0.00: odds ratio 1.165 (1.082–1.255) for a recorded unsafe driver action; 1.28 (1.21–1.36) with only blood alcohol terms in the model; for a male driver aged 45 with no other drugs or driving record the share with a recorded unsafe action rose from about 52 to 56 in 100 (editors' calculation from the printed predicted odds 1.07 and 1.25).

evidence.extracted: Re-analysis of the nine studies of Asbridge et al. and nine of Li et al.: a culpability odds ratio estimates the increase in risk of a culpable crash, higher than the increase in all crashes (a simulation shows the culpability estimator biased upwards); re-extraction changed four of nine Asbridge odds ratios by more than 10%, all downwards (Blows 7.2 to 2.6; Terhune 4.4 to 1.7). Fig 4, read by eye from an enlarged crop (approximate): Asbridge nine studies 1.92 reported, about 1.59 with corrected counts, 1.40 with the adjusted culpability estimator, 1.31 with adjusted estimates from the underlying studies and about 1.25 with both; Li nine studies 2.66 reported, about 1.55 with adjusted estimates. The Discussion (p. 8) says the revised value for the Asbridge studies lies between 1.22 and 1.36. The correction leaves standard errors unreduced (footnote 1); after corrected counts alone the intervals still contain the original 1.92 and 2.66.

evidence.locator: Results › Risk of bias assessment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 6, continued p. 8); Discussion › Alternative interpretations of the results, 1st to 4th paragraphs; Conclusions, 1st paragraph (p. 10)
evidence.extracted: Included studies scored 4.11 of 5 on quality of information on use (excluded studies 2.16); poor measures such as urine tests bias towards no effect, while non-response among roadside controls probably inflates odds ratios; drivers who use cannabis may drive when they judge impairment low (understating risk) and may share traits with higher crash risk such as high speed and drink-driving (overstating it). The authors conclude that acute intoxication is associated with a statistically significant increase in crash risk of low to moderate magnitude and that remaining selection effects may complicate a causal reading. The paper words positive tests as intoxication; no included study measured impairment.

evidence.locator: Results, 6th paragraph; Table 2 (THC Exposure row); Table 3 (BAC .00 row)
evidence.extracted: THC alone at BAC 0.00, final model adjusted for age, sex, BAC, other drug classes and a three-year driving record: B = 0.153 (SE 0.038), OR 1.165 (95% CI 1.082–1.255) for a recorded unsafe driver action among drivers in fatal US crashes (150,010 tested, 3,387 THC only against 87,280 free of alcohol and THC); 1.28 (1.21–1.36) with BAC terms only; predicted odds 1.07 without and 1.25 with THC at BAC .00 for a male driver aged 45 (editors' calculation: about 52 and 56 in 100). The Discussion says this is lower than the 29% from the group's earlier study.

evidence.extracted: The outcome is a police-recorded potentially unsafe driver action in drivers already in a fatal crash, a proxy for responsibility; THC is a yes/no blood marker with no concentration, dose or timing, and can remain in the blood for hours or days, so some THC-positive drivers may not have been impaired (the authors say this would understate the culpability odds); FARS does not say why THC was present.

evidence.extracted: Nine studies of acute cannabis use in drivers (six culpability, three case-control; five fatal collisions, four non-fatal), cannabis-only drivers against drivers with none: pooled odds ratio 1.92 (95% CI 1.35–2.73), P = 0.0003, I-squared 81%; study estimates from 0.82 to 7.16; the authors rate the overall quality of evidence moderate. This pooled value was later revised downwards by re-extraction and adjustment (see the Rogeberg and Elvik anchors); the review is critically low on AMSTAR 2 on its study card.

risk_of_bias.note: The updated meta-analysis is low confidence on AMSTAR 2 on its card (no protocol cited; list of excluded studies not available), the 2012 review critically low; 17 of 28 estimates come from studies with limited or no confounder adjustment; culpability and case-control designs are mixed with a correction that leaves standard errors unreduced; the estimate moves from 1.79 to 1.11 with alcohol control.

inconsistency.note: Not scored: individual estimates run from 0.22 to 13.40 with 9 of 28 below 1 and no heterogeneity statistic printed, but the review explains part of the spread by alcohol control, adjustment and design (Table 3), and the claim gives the figure by method rather than one value; scoring it as well would count the same problem twice.

indirectness.note: None as worded: the claim is about the odds of being in a crash or being judged responsible, among drivers with a positive test, and says a positive test is not impairment.

imprecision.note: Pooled intervals are narrow (1.10–1.61); subgroup contrasts rest on 7 to 17 estimates and are not read finely.

publication_bias.note: PEESE bias test P = 0.52 and trim-and-fill trimmed mean 1.23 (weak bias); the review reports no sign of important small-study effects.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the pooled odds ratios are below 2.

dose_response.note: Not applied: five studies tested a dose-response pattern and three found one, none pooled.

plausible_confounding.note: Not applied: the review's authors name residual confounding that would raise the estimate and selection on effect that would lower it.

grade.reasoning: Observational case-control and culpability studies pooled in a re-analysis read in full, so the claim starts low. Risk of bias −1 (see the domain note); inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias 0; no upgrade. The direction (an odds ratio above 1) holds in every pooled analysis, from 1.11 to 1.36, but the size depends on method and alcohol control, and the claim gives it as a range by method. Relation: is associated with; the authors say remaining selection effects may bias estimates in either direction and the figures concern odds among crashed or at-fault drivers, not risk to a driver. Status: replicated, by several independent primary studies with an odds ratio above 1 (for example Laumon, Li, Brault and Dubois, each with an interval excluding 1) among those pooled. The 2012 review, the 2016 re-analysis and the 2015 US analysis are not independent confirmations of each other: the re-analysis re-extracts the nine studies of the review and includes the US analysis as its heaviest weight, so the three count once. A 2019 culpability-design meta-analysis by the first author of the re-analysis (10.1016/j.aap.2018.11.011) is open access and was not read.

verification.flag_note: Not read: Rogeberg 2019 (culpability-design meta-analysis, 10.1016/j.aap.2018.11.011, open access); Dubois Appendix 1 and Rogeberg Appendix S1 (not in the PDFs); the older simulator and on-road studies of the combination (Robbe 1998, Ramaekers 2000, Lamers 2001, Lenné 2010, Ronen 2010), known only from how Hartman and Dubois describe them; Li et al. 2012, Elvik 2013 and Bédard 2007; the Hartman supplements and registry record (NCT01620177); the Thai companion papers on subjective and cognitive effects; Liechti 2006 and Miró 2017 on GHB with alcohol. No study read asks whether drivers or patients felt impaired (Ronen 2010 on perceived effects and Verster and Roth 2012 on drivers' own predictions are named in the Hartman reference list). The three sources count once for replication: they share primary studies.
